KEY MESSAGE 1...As of 3:10 AM EDT...Current sfc analysis shows 
a 1014 mb sfc high located over western NY building eastwards. 
With mainly clear skies and diminishing winds, this has allowed 
for favorable radiational cooling conditions with temperatures 
in the 40s to 50 per latest NYS mesonet and ASOS obs. Some 
patchy radiation fog is expected through early this morning, but
should dissipate quickly after sunrise. High pressure remains 
overhead today, resulting in a quiet weather day with with highs
climbing into the upper 70s to low 80s under mostly clear 
skies. Low humidity will make for a very comfortable day. 

Tonight, a low 990s mb sfc low will track across Ontario and into 
Quebec in association with an potent upper trough. The system's warm 
front will attempt to lift northwards through the region Tuesday, 
but likely remains hung up to our south until late Tuesday 
afternoon or early evening. Once it lifts north, this will 
briefly place southern portions of our region in the warm sector
before an initial cold front tracks through the region Tuesday 
night. Some showers and perhaps a few rumbles of thunder will be
possible with the warm advection/isentropic lift Tuesday 
morning and early afternoon. There is a better chance for 
thunderstorms in the evening and early Wednesday night ahead of 
the cold front, but the severe weather potential looks quite 
muddled at this time... 

Low-level and deep-layer wind shear both look quite impressive with 
long curved hodographs. However, instability looks to be a limiting 
factor with <500 J/kg of SBCAPE for most of the region, except near 
the I-84 corridor where 500-1000 J/kg is possible in the narrow warm
sector Tuesday evening. BUFKIT model soundings also show quite 
a bit of CIN and weak mid-level lapse rates, even for areas in 
the warm sector. The other limiting factor is that this initial
cold front doesn't arrive until after sunset. Upper forcing 
looks quite strong, but we don't have a lot of confidence that
this will be able to compensate for this myriad of limiting 
factors. SPC has expanded the slight risk to include the ADKs, 
Capital District, and areas south and west, but this seems quite
aggressive given the lack of instability and capping inversion 
that will be in place. Our thinking is that the highest chance 
for severe weather is for the I-84 corridor, southeastern 
Catskills, and far western Mohawk Valley, with only a low chance
for the rest of the region. 

Some locally heavy rain appears possible Tuesday afternoon into 
Tuesday night with warm cloud depths around 12 kft and PWATs 
approaching 2". Storm motions looks fast, although some 
training/backbuilding of storms will be possible with flow 
aloft parallel to the approaching cold frontal boundary. 00z 
HREF is showing a 10% chance for 3" of rain in 3 hrs across the 
Mid Hudson Valley, eastern Catskills, and southwestern New 
England Tuesday afternoon. This is a fairly strong signal for
heavy rain, so it will be something to keep an eye on. This 
area did see around an inch of rain a couple days ago, but 
having a couple of dry days combined with ongoing rainfall 
deficits should help lower the risk of hydro issues outside of 
the urban areas. WPC has placed our region in a marginal risk 
ERO Tuesday, but heavy rain threat appears highest for the 
southern half of the CWA. 

For Wednesday, the deeper moisture will have been pushed off to our 
east by the Tuesday night cold frontal passage, but some guidance 
suggests we may see another surge of warm/moist air ahead of 
the next (and much stronger) cold front. Timing of the front 
looks too early for much of a severe threat for our western 
areas, but western New England and possibly the Taconics may see
enough instability for a few stronger storms. For these areas, 
deep-layer shear still looks fairly impressive with 30-40 kt, 
although hodographs are much straighter compared to Tuesday. 
Guidance has trended slightly slower with this cold front over 
the last few runs, and if this trend continues then that could 
increase the severe threat Wednesday. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...Behind the cold front, sfc high pressure builds over 
the region Thursday and Friday under W/NW flow and very weak, broad 
upper troughing. This will result in tranquil weather. Temperatures 
Thursday may end up a few degrees below normal, but should warm to 
near normal levels Friday with heights aloft continuing to rise. 
Tranquil weather should continue into next weekend with a lack of 
synoptic forcing, although temperatures and humidity begin to 
nudge upward Saturday and Sunday as the sfc high slides off to 
our east.
